newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Hoechst plummets as HMR plan shelved.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Hoechst plummets as HMR plan shelved.

text.p: German chemicals and drugs group Hoechst AG on Wednesday disappointed markets by shelving plans to list its drugs subsidiary HMR but insisted the decision did not reflect a change in strategy.

After quickly establishing itself as a market favourite under the dynamic leadership of management board chairman Juergen Dormann, Hoechst dismayed investors when it said it would no longer list the Hoechst Marion Roussel unit.

Shares plummeted in pre-bourse trade after Dormann officially announced the decision which had been rumoured for a number of months. In bourse trade, the stock started at 70.40 marks, down 8.15 marks or more than 10 percent from Tuesday's floor trade finish.
"We see bringing HMR to the stock market as no longer in the best interests of our shareholders," Juergen Dormann told analysts in a morning video conference.
However he stressed, "this should not be seen as a change in our strategy."
But the market did not share his view, especially after analysts warned that any distancing from the plan to float HMR would be seen as negative.
The comments were made in a conference call with analysts to which Reuters had access.
Analysts said the news was received with scepticism and that several might consider downgrading Hoechst.

To keep the market interest alive, Hoechst stressed that it would continue to strengthen its drugs division and was receptive to potential mergers or other takeovers. The group bought U.S. drugs group Marion Merrell Dow in 1994.

Dormann also said that Hoechst could possibly accelerate the pace of restructuring which saw the group divest itself of a number of businesses last year. Analysts said that now that it had sold its specialty chemicals group to Clariant, Hoechst would likely sell its generic drugs business Copley soon.
Hoechst said it was considering a variety of options for the business, especially after the Copley unit incurred a loss of 19 million marks ($11 million) in 1996.

"Hoechst is trying hard to keep fantasies alive now," said Ronald Koehler, analyst at BHF Bank, but he declined to comment on whether the group, which had so successfully positioned its shares in recent months, could do the same now.

On Tuesday Hoechst disappointed markets by reporting a 2.5 percent drop in sale to 50.9 billion marks and saying it pre-tax profit climbed by 29.06 percent to 5.28 billion marks, largely due to earnings from divestments.
The group raised its dividend to 1.40 marks from 1.30 marks, a similarly disappointing result after dealers had hoped for a much heftier increase.
On the other hand, Hoechst said it still planned to list Hoechst AG shares on the New York bourse, so becoming only the third big German company after Daimler Benz and Telecom to do so.
